objectives: Recognize when real-time scheduling is needed.

slides.title: Scheduling — the problem, classic algorithms, and pathologies
slides.body:
The CPU scheduler is the kernel subsystem that decides which thread runs on which CPU core at every moment. With $N$ runnable threads and $C$ cores where $N \gg C$, the choice of scheduling algorithm profoundly affects throughput, latency, fairness, and responsiveness.

**Cooperative vs preemptive scheduling.**
- **Cooperative scheduling**: threads voluntarily yield control (e.g., by calling `yield()` or blocking on I/O). Simple to implement; catastrophic when any thread misbehaves or loops without yielding. Used in early single-user systems, MS-DOS, and early Mac OS. Also used in user-space concurrency: Go goroutines, Python asyncio, Lua coroutines all cooperate at the language level while the OS provides preemption beneath them.
- **Preemptive scheduling**: the kernel sets a hardware timer (the **scheduler tick**, typically 1–10 ms, configured by `CONFIG_HZ` in Linux); when the timer fires, an interrupt preempts the running thread and the scheduler decides whether to switch. Every modern multi-user OS kernel is preemptive — fairness is guaranteed even against poorly-written or malicious code.

**Classic scheduling algorithms:**

**FCFS (First Come First Served).** Threads run in arrival order, to completion. Zero starvation. Terrible for interactive use: a CPU-bound batch job arriving first delays all subsequent short interactive tasks. Exhibits the **convoy effect**: one long job causes a train of short jobs to queue behind it, drastically reducing average response time.

**Round-Robin (RR).** Each thread gets a fixed **time slice** (also called **quantum**) — typically 10–100 ms — then is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue. Trivially fair for equal-priority tasks. Response time scales linearly with queue length: with 100 threads each needing 10 ms, the 100th thread waits 990 ms for its first slice. Quantum size is a fundamental trade-off: small quantum = responsive but high context-switch overhead; large quantum = efficient but sluggish.

**Shortest Job First (SJF) / Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF).** Provably minimizes average waiting time (proven by **Edward Coffman** and **Leonard Kleinrock** in early scheduling theory). The catch: requires knowing job duration in advance, which is generally impossible. SRTF (preemptive SJF) can cause **starvation** of long jobs if short jobs keep arriving.

**Priority scheduling.** Each thread has a priority; the highest-priority runnable thread always runs. Used in real-time systems and OS internals. Vulnerable to **starvation**: a low-priority thread may never run if high-priority threads continuously exist. Mitigation: **aging** — gradually increase the priority of waiting threads (proposed by **Raphael Rom** and others in the 1970s).

**Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ).** Proposed by **Fernando Corbató** at MIT for the CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System) in the 1960s, for which Corbató won the 1990 Turing Award. MLFQ uses multiple queues with different priorities and time quanta. New threads enter the highest-priority queue (short quantum, good for interactive tasks). If a thread uses its entire quantum without blocking, it is demoted to a lower-priority queue (longer quantum, treated as a batch job). I/O-bound threads that give up CPU before their quantum expires stay at high priority. MLFQ approximates SJF without requiring advance knowledge of job length — the scheduler *infers* job type from behavior. The Linux MLFQ variant uses **nice values** to adjust priority.

slides.title: Linux CFS — the Completely Fair Scheduler
slides.body:
The Linux **Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS)** was written by **Ingo Molnar** and merged into the Linux kernel in version **2.6.23** (released October 2007), replacing the earlier O(1) scheduler (designed by Ingo Molnar in 2002 for kernel 2.5.2) and the O(n) scheduler it replaced. CFS has been the default Linux scheduler for all normal tasks ever since.

**The core invariant.** CFS does not use fixed time quanta. Instead, it tracks how much CPU time each runnable task has consumed (weighted by priority), expressed as **virtual runtime (vruntime)** in nanoseconds. Vruntime advances faster for lower-priority (higher nice value) tasks and slower for higher-priority tasks. CFS always schedules the task with the **lowest vruntime** — the task that has received the least CPU time proportionally. This ensures that over any interval, every task receives exactly its fair share of CPU time.

**Priority weighting.** Nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest priority), default 0. CFS maps nice values to **weights** using a precomputed table: nice 0 → weight 1024; each +1 nice step multiplies weight by approximately $1/1.25$ (so nice +5 ≈ weight 335, nice +10 ≈ weight 110). A task's CPU share is $w_i / \sum_j w_j$. A nice -5 task gets roughly 3× the CPU of a nice +0 task sharing the same core.

**Red-black tree implementation.** CFS stores all runnable tasks in a **red-black tree** (self-balancing BST) keyed by vruntime. The task with the smallest vruntime is always the leftmost node, cached in `cfs_rq->rb_leftmost`. Scheduling a new task: pop the leftmost node, run it for a scheduling slice, update its vruntime, re-insert into the tree. Insert/delete/find-minimum are all $O(\log N)$. For $N = 100$ runnable tasks, that's ~7 comparisons per scheduling decision — entirely acceptable.

**Scheduling slice and latency tuning.** The kernel tries to give every runnable task a turn within `sched_latency_ns` (default 6 ms, configurable in `/proc/sys/kernel/sched_latency_ns`). Each task's slice is `sched_latency_ns × w_i / \sum w_j`. No task runs for less than `sched_min_granularity_ns` (default 750 µs). On a heavily loaded interactive desktop (many tasks), latency per task increases; tuning `sched_latency_ns` downward improves responsiveness at the cost of more context switches.

**Context switch overhead.** Each context switch requires saving the current thread's register state (general-purpose registers, FPU/SIMD state, segment registers) and restoring the next thread's state, then switching page tables if the new thread is in a different process (TLB flush or PCID tag switch). On modern hardware, a context switch costs ~1–10 µs. With Spectre/Meltdown mitigations (KPTI), inter-process context switches are more expensive than intra-process (thread) switches.

**NUMA-aware scheduling.** On multi-socket servers with **Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA)** topology, CFS performs **load balancing** across CPUs in two phases: (1) periodic load balancing via the `load_balance()` function called on scheduler ticks; (2) idle balancing when a CPU becomes idle. CFS tries to keep threads on their preferred NUMA node (the one with their memory) to minimize memory-access latency. `numactl` and `taskset` allow manual CPU and memory affinity pinning.

slides.title: Real-time scheduling — deadlines, rate-monotonic, and EDF
slides.body:
CFS provides statistical fairness; it provides no deadline guarantees. Many systems require **real-time scheduling**: the guarantee that a task will complete within a specified time bound. Examples: audio production (a sample must be rendered every 23 µs at 44.1 kHz), flight control, automotive safety systems, industrial motion controllers.

**Theoretical foundations.** The seminal theoretical framework for real-time scheduling was established by **C. L. Liu** and **James W. Layland** in their 1973 paper "Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard Real-Time Environment" (Journal of the ACM, 1973). Liu and Layland analyzed a model of $N$ periodic tasks, each with a period $T_i$ and worst-case execution time $C_i$, and proved:

- **Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS)**: assign static priorities in inverse proportion to period (shorter period = higher priority). RMS is **optimal among fixed-priority algorithms** — if any fixed-priority assignment can meet all deadlines, RMS will. The utilization bound for $N$ tasks is $U = \sum_{i=1}^N C_i / T_i \leq N(2^{1/N} - 1)$, which approaches $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$ as $N \to \infty$. Tasks are schedulable under RMS if total utilization is below ~69.3%.

- **Earliest Deadline First (EDF)**: a dynamic-priority algorithm that always runs the task with the nearest absolute deadline. EDF is **optimal among all scheduling algorithms** for periodic tasks on a single CPU: it can schedule any set of tasks with total utilization $U \leq 1.0$ (100% CPU utilization). The proof by Liu and Layland is a classic of the field.

**Linux real-time scheduling classes.** Linux provides three real-time scheduling classes, which preempt all CFS tasks:

- **SCHED_FIFO**: fixed priority (1–99, where 99 is highest). The thread runs until it blocks, calls `sched_yield()`, or a higher-priority SCHED_FIFO thread becomes runnable. No preemption between equal-priority SCHED_FIFO threads. A buggy SCHED_FIFO thread that spins without blocking will lock out the entire system. Used by: JACK audio server, PipeWire, hardware ISR threads, real-time networking stacks.

- **SCHED_RR** (Round-Robin): like SCHED_FIFO but equal-priority threads time-slice among themselves (default quantum: 100 ms).

- **SCHED_DEADLINE** (CBS — Constant Bandwidth Server, Linux 3.14, 2014): each task declares a `(runtime, deadline, period)` tuple. The kernel uses an EDF-like algorithm to guarantee the declared runtime within the declared deadline, and applies admission control — the kernel refuses to admit a new SCHED_DEADLINE task if it would cause existing tasks to miss deadlines. Used in some automotive and industrial Linux deployments.

**The `RLIMIT_RTTIME` safety valve.** A process running under SCHED_FIFO that consumes more than `RLIMIT_RTTIME` microseconds of CPU time without blocking receives a SIGKILL, preventing runaway RT threads from permanently locking the system.

**Starvation and the convoy effect in practice.** In a production system, starvation occurs when low-priority threads never get CPU because high-priority threads are always runnable. CFS's vruntime mechanism prevents starvation among CFS tasks. The **convoy effect** (terminology from **Michael Blasgen**, **Jim Gray**, **Mike Mitoma**, **Tom Price**, 1977 IBM paper on database locking) refers to a single slow holder blocking a queue of faster tasks — visible in any FCFS queue and in database lock convoys. Solutions: preemption, priority inheritance (for lock convoys), or load balancing across queues.

question.question: Derive CFS fair-share allocation
question.goal: Two tasks: A nice=0 (weight 1024), B nice=5 (weight 335). Both runnable. CPU share?

steps.prompt: CFS allocates CPU in proportion to weight. Each task's share = its_weight / sum_of_weights. A's share?
steps.reveal: A gets 1024/1359 ≈ 75% of CPU; B gets 335/1359 ≈ 25%. So A gets ~3× B's CPU.

steps.prompt: If a third task C nice=10 (weight 110) joins, A's new share?
steps.reveal: A drops to 1024/1469 ≈ 70%. CFS smoothly re-allocates as the runnable set changes.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{CFS share}_i = w_i / \sum_j w_j}$$ Proportional fair share. nice values map to weights; each +1 nice = ~1.25× less weight (so +5 nice = ~3× less weight than +0). Fairness is over the long run; short-term latency depends on tunables.

question.question: An audio app needs to produce a sample every 23µs without dropouts. Best scheduling class:
options: SCHED_FIFO — preempts CFS; audio thread runs whenever it has work.
question.explanation: Audio has hard latency requirements. CFS guarantees fairness, not low latency. SCHED_FIFO preempts CFS; the audio thread runs immediately when it has work. JACK, PipeWire, professional audio stacks all use SCHED_FIFO. The cost: if the audio code has a bug that doesn't block/yield, the system can hang — so SCHED_FIFO requires careful audit.

hints: What scheduling class can preempt the CFS scheduler entirely?
Real-time scheduling classes (FIFO, RR, DEADLINE) sit above CFS.
slides.workedSolution: SCHED_FIFO threads run whenever runnable, preempting all CFS. Audio production: assign the audio thread SCHED_FIFO at priority ~70. Now even a busy desktop won't introduce audio dropouts. JACK, PipeWire, ALSA all do this. Caveat: misbehaving SCHED_FIFO threads can lock the system; only use for thoroughly-tested code.

question.question: Tail latency under load
question.prompt: Your gRPC service runs fine at low load; under load, p99 latency jumps from 5ms to 200ms. CPU usage is only 60%. Walk through the most likely scheduling-related cause + how you'd verify it.
Explain in two or three sentences why kernel preemptive scheduling can't be replaced by language-level cooperative coroutines in a general-purpose OS.
question.rubric: Mentions that cooperative scheduling relies on every runnable entity to yield; one uncooperative entity blocks everyone else; in a multi-user/multi-app OS you can't trust every app to yield correctly; kernel preemption forces fairness.
